families.s: HSE agricultural grain-dust respiratory-risk and exposure-control guidance
families.t: harvesting, drying, handling, storage, contaminants, enclosure, extraction, cab filtration, cleaning, RPE and surveillance
f: Grain dust arises during harvesting, drying, handling, storage and processing of cereal crops.
It can contain bacteria, endotoxin, fungal spores, insects, debris and pesticide residues.
Agricultural grain-dust exposure is associated with occupational asthma and other respiratory disease.
The workplace exposure limit does not replace the duty to keep exposure as low as reasonably practicable.
Enclosure and extraction should control dust at transfer, tipping, conveying and cleaning points.
Effective filters in tractor or vehicle cabs can reduce exposure during dusty operations.
Dry sweeping and uncontrolled compressed-air cleaning should be avoided where they spread dust.
Suitable RPE, instruction, maintenance and health surveillance may be needed where residual risk remains.
families.g: Grain-dust risk depends on crop and contamination, moisture, task, dustiness, enclosure, extraction, cab filtration, cleaning, duration, RPE and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE agricultural pesticide authorisation, storage, handling and application guidance
families.t: authorised products, secure stores, transport, labels, application equipment, exposure, PPE, spills and disposal
f: Only pesticides authorised for storage and use in the UK should be purchased and used.
Fixed and mobile pesticide stores should meet suitable security, containment, ventilation and segregation standards.
Pesticides should not be carried in the cab of tractors or other vehicles.
Users should follow the product label and applicable conditions of authorisation.
Application equipment should be suitable, maintained and calibrated for the intended product and use.
Risk assessment should cover mixing, loading, spraying, cleaning, storage, transport and disposal.
Engineering controls, closed transfer, suitable PPE and RPE should be selected from the exposure assessment.
Spill, contamination, emergency and waste arrangements should be established before work starts.
families.g: Pesticide risk depends on product authorisation and hazard, formulation, dose, equipment, weather, route, operator exposure, storage, PPE, cleaning and disposal.

families.s: HSE chainsaw selection, competence, maintenance and safe-work guidance
families.t: training, competence, fitness, selection, maintenance, PPE, felling, off-ground use, first aid and lone work
f: Chainsaws can cause fatal or major injury when they are selected or used incorrectly.
Anyone using a chainsaw at work should be trained and competent for the type of work required.
Work planning should cover the saw, chain, timber, felling method, terrain, weather and people nearby.
Chainsaws should be inspected and maintained so safety features and cutting components remain effective.
Appropriate chainsaw PPE includes protection selected for the task and whether work is on the ground or aerial.
Off-ground chainsaw use requires specific training and safe working techniques.
First-aid provision should reflect the severity and remoteness of foreseeable injuries.
Lone-working arrangements should account for communication, location, emergency access and rescue time.
families.g: Chainsaw risk depends on saw and chain, timber, cut, terrain, weather, competence, PPE, maintenance, felling plan, other people and emergency response.

families.s: HSE aerial tree-work, climbing, lifting and rescue guidance
families.t: two-person teams, aerial rescue, ropes, communication, public exclusion, chainsaw competence, PPE and dynamic reassessment
f: Aerial tree work is hazardous and is subject to work-at-height and lifting-equipment duties.
At least two people should be present during aerial work.
A competent and equipped member of the ground team should be available to perform aerial rescue without delay.
Climbers and chainsaw users need training and competence for the work they undertake.
Ground staff should maintain communication and keep climbing and work ropes clear of machinery and obstructions.
Public and traffic exclusion controls should remain effective throughout the operation.
Pre-work checks should cover the tree, anchor points, equipment, weather, drop zone and rescue arrangements.
The work plan and risk assessment should be revised when conditions or the operation change.
families.g: Aerial-tree-work risk depends on tree condition, anchors, ropes, equipment, climber and ground-team competence, weather, public exclusion, communication and rescue.

families.s: HSE woodchipper, stump-grinder, brushcutter and forestry-machinery guidance
families.t: training, guarding, feed systems, exclusion zones, maintenance, isolation, noise, vibration and thrown objects
f: Tree-work machinery includes woodchippers, brushcutters, stump grinders, flails and mulchers.
No one should use this equipment unless trained and competent.
Risk assessment should cover dangerous moving parts, feed systems, thrown objects and machine stability.
Guards, emergency stops and other protective devices should remain effective.
Blockage clearance, cleaning and maintenance require shutdown and effective isolation.
Exclusion zones should protect workers and the public from ejected material and moving equipment.
Noise and vibration exposure should be assessed and reduced.
Machine selection should account for site access, terrain, timber size, work position and manufacturer instructions.
families.g: Tree-machinery risk depends on machine type, guarding, feed material, terrain, exclusion, maintenance, isolation, competence, noise and vibration.

families.s: HSE waste and recyclable collection, bin and refuse-vehicle guidance
families.t: collection routes, people in bins, moving machinery, manual handling, hoists, public interaction, communication and emergency stop
f: Waste collection exposes workers and the public to moving vehicles, machinery, lifting and manual-handling hazards.
Collection businesses should have arrangements to identify people before large bins are emptied.
Crews should know how to stop the compactor immediately if a person is tipped into a vehicle.
Hoists fitted to refuse vehicles and other lifting equipment require suitable inspection and control.
Collection routes should account for traffic, reversing, visibility and access to bins.
Workers need safe systems for moving, positioning and emptying containers.
Public interaction, including foreseeable aggression, should be included in planning and training.
Communication between drivers and crew is required around blind spots, machinery and vehicle movement.
families.g: Waste-collection risk depends on route, vehicle, bin type, public presence, reversing, hoists, compactor, manual handling, crew communication and emergency controls.
